mcqs.question: A consumer can't keep up with its producer. What determines the right fix?
options: Which of buffering, scaling consumers, slowing the producer, or shedding actually addresses where the real bottleneck lives
Always adding more consumer instances, since that fixes any throughput gap
Always increasing the queue's retention period
Always switching the queue technology to one with higher advertised throughput
mcqs.explanation: There's no single universal fix — the right lever depends on whether the bottleneck is consumer count, a downstream dependency, or a burst the producer could tolerate slowing for. Always scaling consumers, extending retention, or switching technology are one-size-fits-all reactions that ignore where the actual constraint sits.

mcqs.question: A consumer is backlogged, but its real bottleneck is a downstream database capped at 200 writes/sec. What happens if you scale the consumer pool 10x?
options: Throughput increases roughly 10x, matching the new consumer count
Throughput stays capped near 200/sec — the extra pods just shift pressure onto the database's connection pool instead of fixing anything
The database automatically scales its write capacity to match the new consumer count
The queue depth increases because more consumers compete for the same messages
mcqs.explanation: When the downstream dependency is the actual ceiling, more consumer pods don't add usable throughput — they just pile more concurrent callers onto a database that still tops out at 200 writes/sec. Databases don't auto-scale from consumer count alone, and more consumers reading a queue doesn't itself increase queue depth.

mcqs.question: How do you tell a temporary traffic burst apart from a permanent capacity problem when queue depth spikes?
options: A single alarm firing is enough to conclude it's permanent
Trend queue depth over the autoscaling window — sustained growth despite being at max scale-out signals a real capacity ceiling, not a blip
Permanent problems always correlate with a specific time of day
There's no reliable way to distinguish the two before an outage occurs
mcqs.explanation: Watching the trend across the full autoscaling window shows whether depth recovers as pods scale out (a burst) or keeps climbing even at maximum scale (a real ceiling). A single alarm is too noisy to conclude either way, time-of-day correlation isn't a reliable signal, and there is a concrete way to distinguish them before things get catastrophic.

mcqs.question: A team lets its backlog queue grow without any depth limit, reasoning "it'll just absorb whatever comes in." What's the risk?
options: None — unbounded queues are the safest configuration for absorbing bursts
The queue automatically starts dropping the newest messages once memory is tight
It delays and hides the failure — memory grows until the consumer OOMs, or staleness quietly breaches an SLA unnoticed until it's already broken
The producer will automatically slow down once the queue passes a certain size
mcqs.explanation: Without a depth limit, growth continues invisibly until something breaks outright — an OOM crash or an SLA violation nobody caught in time. Queues don't auto-drop or auto-throttle the producer on their own; that behavior has to be built deliberately as a depth limit with a shedding policy.
